title: El vs Él: The Accent That Changes “The” to “He”
seo_title: El vs Él: The Accent That Changes “The” to “He”
meta_description: El vs él: el is the article “the”, él with an accent is the pronoun “he” or “him”. Simple rules, examples, contractions and capital letters, with a quiz.
excerpt: One little accent turns “the” into “he”. Here is how to get it right every time.

body_html:
El vs él is one of the first accent pairs Spanish learners meet, and one of the easiest to fix. El without an accent is the masculine article, “the”: el libro, el carro. Él with an accent is the pronoun “he” or “him”: Él es mi hermano (He is my brother), Voy con él (I’m going with him). They sound exactly the same, so the accent is the only way a reader can tell them apart.

Quick answer
  • El = the (before a masculine noun): el perro.
  • Él = he or him: Él trabaja aquí, para él.
  • Test: if you can replace it with “he” or “him”, it needs the accent.
  • Contractions al and del come from el, never from él: de él.
{{toc}}

El vs él: the core rule

elél
Type of wordArticleSubject or object pronoun
Englishthehe, him
What followsA noun, or an adjective + nounUsually a verb, or nothing
ExampleEl doctor llegó tarde.Él llegó tarde.

This accent is called a diacritical accent, or tilde diacrítica. It doesn’t change pronunciation; it only separates two words that are spelled alike. The Real Academia Española lists all of these pairs in its Diccionario panhispánico de dudas.

When to write el

Write el without an accent whenever it means “the”:

  • el café, el lunes, el problema
  • el mejor día de mi vida the best day of my life
  • el que llegue primero whoever arrives first
  • el agua, el águila: feminine nouns that start with a stressed a still take el in the singular

Remember the two contractions: a + el = al and de + el = del. Voy al mercado, la casa del vecino.

{{image:2}}

When to write él

Write él with an accent whenever it means “he” or “him”:

  • As a subject: Él no sabe nada. He doesn’t know anything.
  • After a preposition: Hablé con él. Esto es para él. Confío en él.
  • For contrast or emphasis: Yo cocino y él lava los platos.
  • With mismo: Lo hizo él mismo. He did it himself.

Because Spanish often drops subject pronouns, you will see él mostly after prepositions or when the speaker wants to make it clear who is meant. See {{link:subject-pronouns-in-spanish|subject pronouns in Spanish}}.

Contractions: del and al, but de él

This is where many learners slip. The contractions only work with the article:

  • Es la casa del profesor. It’s the teacher’s house. (de + el)
  • Es la casa de él. It’s his house. (no contraction)
  • Voy al banco. I’m going to the bank. (a + el)
  • Se lo di a él. I gave it to him. (no contraction)

Never write “dél”. If you see de él or a él, the pronoun is keeping its own identity.

{{book:a-road-in-bloom}}

Capital letters keep their accent

A common myth says capital letters don’t need accents in Spanish. They do. At the start of a sentence you write Él es médico, with the accent on the capital É. On a phone or a laptop, hold down the E key or use the international keyboard to get it.

Missing accents on capitals are especially common in headlines and signs, which is why learners see them so often. Don’t copy that habit.

Why el vs él matters

In speech, nobody hears the accent, and context makes the meaning obvious. In writing, a missing accent forces the reader to stop and reread. Compare El trabajo (the job) with Él trabajó (he worked): the accent on the pronoun and the one on the verb completely change the sentence.

In my experience reviewing translations, a missing accent on él is one of the first things a Spanish-speaking reader notices. It is a small error, but in an email, a résumé or a school essay it makes the writing look careless. The good news is that it is also one of the easiest to fix, because the test is so simple.

{{image:3}}

Common mistakes

  • Hablé con el. After a preposition it means “him”: Hablé con él.
  • Él perro de mi vecino ladra mucho. Before a noun it means “the”: El perro…
  • El es de México. As a subject meaning “he”: Él es de México.
  • Es el regalo dél. No contraction with the pronoun: Es el regalo de él, or simply Es su regalo.

The same logic applies to {{link:tu-vs-tu|tu vs tú}} and {{link:si-vs-si|si vs sí}}, and the rules for all accents are in {{link:spanish-accent-marks|Spanish accent marks}}.

Practice: fix the message

Here is a text message with the accents missing. Try to fix it before reading the answer.

El me dijo que el restaurante estaba cerrado. Fui con el a buscar otro, pero el problema es que el no tenía hambre.

Corrected: Él me dijo que el restaurante estaba cerrado. Fui con él a buscar otro, pero el problema es que él no tenía hambre. He told me the restaurant was closed. I went with him to find another one, but the problem is he wasn’t hungry.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

El vs él is a two-second check: if you can say “he” or “him”, add the accent. Get this one right and the other accent pairs will feel much easier. For every other pair that confuses learners, see {{link:spanish-confusing-words|Spanish confusing words}}.

faq.q: What is the difference between el and él?
faq.a: El is the article “the”. Él with an accent is the pronoun “he” or “him”.

faq.q: Do capital letters need accents in Spanish?
faq.a: Yes. Write Él with an accent at the start of a sentence.
Del when it means “of the”: la casa del vecino. De él when it means “his”: la casa de él.

faq.q: Does the accent change the pronunciation?
faq.a: No. El and él sound the same; the accent only distinguishes their meaning in writing.
